item.title: Australian travel industry hits out at Fiji tourism tax rollout
item.description: Australia’s peak travel industry body has criticised the rollout of Fiji’s new five per cent tourism tax, warning its application to existing bookings could leave travellers facing unexpected additional costs. The Australian Travel Industry Association (ATIA) says the tax, which takes effect from September 1, should not be retrospectively applied to holidays already booked and paid for.
item.content:encoded:
Australia’s peak travel industry body has criticised the rollout of Fiji’s new five per cent tourism tax, warning its application to existing bookings could leave travellers facing unexpected additional costs.

The Australian Travel Industry Association (ATIA) says the tax, which takes effect from September 1, should not be retrospectively applied to holidays already booked and paid for.

“The design and rollout reflect a complete lack of understanding of how the travel booking ecosystem works, and it is travellers and travel businesses who will pay the price for that failure,” ATIA chief executive officer Dean Long said.

“Retrospective application is an absolute no-go. Once a customer has paid, that price is locked in.”

Mr Long said asking customers to pay additional charges after completing their bookings amounted to “a broken promise dressed up as policy”.

He said travellers were now being asked to find additional money for holidays they believed had been fully paid for months earlier.

“That is not how you treat people who chose Fiji in good faith,” he said.

ATIA has also criticised what it says was a lack of consultation with the Australian and New Zealand travel industries before the tax changes were announced.

“None of this needed to happen. The tax arrived with zero consultation with the travel industry in Australia or New Zealand despite the significant importance of these markets to Fiji,” Mr Long said.

He said Australia was Fiji’s largest tourism market and New Zealand its second-largest, yet the industry was given just over two weeks between the announcement and implementation of the tax.

Mr Long said this provided insufficient time for businesses to update contracts and pricing systems or properly advise travellers.

The Travel Agents’ Association of New Zealand has raised similar concerns and is calling for existing bookings to be exempt from the new tax.

“Grandfathering existing bookings is the fairest outcome,” TAANZ chief executive officer Julie White said.

“It protects travellers who purchased in good faith, gives the travel industry certainty and allows the new tax to be implemented cleanly for new bookings from 1 September.”

From September 1, the five per cent tax is set to apply to tourism operators, including hotel, tourism and cruise businesses, with annual turnover above $2 million .

The measure forms part of taxation changes announced under Fiji’s 2026-2027 National Budget.

item.title: Bill proposes 16-member Fiji Yaqona Council
item.description: A 16-member Fiji Yaqona Council comprising government and private sector representatives would be established under the Yaqona (Kava) Bill 2026 tabled in Parliament yesterday. The proposed legislation establishes the Fiji Yaqona Council as a corporate body with powers to oversee its affairs, own and dispose of property, enter into contracts, appoint agents and engage consultants.
item.content:encoded:
A 16-member Fiji Yaqona Council comprising government and private sector representatives would be established under the Yaqona (Kava) Bill 2026 tabled in Parliament yesterday.

The proposed legislation establishes the Fiji Yaqona Council as a corporate body with powers to oversee its affairs, own and dispose of property, enter into contracts, appoint agents and engage consultants.

Under the Bill, the Council would consist of eight ex-officio government members and eight representatives from the private sector, all appointed by the Minister.

The Permanent Secretary would serve as chairperson of the Council.

Other government representatives would include officials responsible for commerce, health, rural and maritime development, foreign affairs and iTaukei affairs.

The Chief Executive Officer of the Biosecurity Authority of Fiji, or a representative, would also sit on the Council.

Private sector representation would comprise four members nominated by the Yaqona Working Group and four additional yaqona operators.

The relevant sectors or bodies would nominate their representatives, with the Minister appointing members from among those nominated.

Private sector members would be appointed for terms of up to three years and would be eligible for reappointment.

However, they would not be permitted to serve for more than six consecutive years.

Ex-officio members would remain on the Council for as long as they held the government position through which they were appointed.

Members would also be able to resign by providing the Minister with at least 30 days’ written notice.

The proposed Council would have the legal capacity to sue and be sued, purchase and hold property, sell or lease property and enter into contracts.

It would also be able to appoint agents and attorneys, engage consultants and set charges and other terms for services and facilities it provides.

The Council would have its own common seal, with documents requiring the seal to be signed by the Chief Executive or another duly authorised person.

The establishment of the Council forms part of the broader regulatory framework proposed under the Yaqona (Kava) Bill 2026.

item.title: Bill proposes removal of political donation limits
item.description: Political parties and election candidates could receive unlimited donations under proposed changes contained in the Political Parties (Registration, Conduct, Funding and Disclosures) (Amendment) Bill 2026. Clause 8 of the Bill proposes amending section 22 of the existing Act by removing the current limit on donations that may be received by a political party or candidate.
item.content:encoded:
Political parties and election candidates could receive unlimited donations under proposed changes contained in the Political Parties (Registration, Conduct, Funding and Disclosures) (Amendment) Bill 2026.

Clause 8 of the Bill proposes amending section 22 of the existing Act by removing the current limit on donations that may be received by a political party or candidate.

The proposed amendment would also allow non-Fiji citizens and former Fiji citizens to make donations to political parties and candidates.

Under the proposed changes, however, those donors would be required to declare their donations to the Registrar within 60 days after polling day.

The Registrar would then be required to publish the declaration on the Registrar’s website.

The amendment specifically proposes deleting several subsections of section 22 and changing the wording in subsection (3) from “shall not” to “may”.

It would also insert a requirement that a person making such a donation declare it to the Registrar within the prescribed 60-day period.

The Bill’s explanatory note states that Clause 8 removes both the donation limit and the prohibition on donations from non-Fiji citizens and former Fiji citizens.

The proposed changes represent a significant shift in Fiji’s political financing framework, while retaining a disclosure requirement for donations covered by the amended provision.

The Political Parties (Registration, Conduct, Funding and Disclosures) (Amendment) Bill 2026 was tabled in Parliament as part of wider proposed reforms to Fiji’s electoral laws.

item.title: Yaqona operators to be registered and licensed under new Bill
item.description: Yaqona operators in Fiji would be required to be registered and licensed by the proposed Fiji Yaqona Council under the Yaqona (Kava) Bill 2026. The Bill, tabled in Parliament yesterday, gives the proposed Council wide-ranging functions covering the cultivation, processing, transportation, marketing and export of yaqona.
item.content:encoded:
Yaqona operators in Fiji would be required to be registered and licensed by the proposed Fiji Yaqona Council under the Yaqona (Kava) Bill 2026.

The Bill, tabled in Parliament yesterday, gives the proposed Council wide-ranging functions covering the cultivation, processing, transportation, marketing and export of yaqona.

A key responsibility of the Council would be to “register and licence Yaqona operators” as part of a new regulatory framework for the industry.

The Council would also be required to develop and implement initiatives, guidelines and standards regulating the cultivation, processing and transportation of yaqona, as well as its international trade and marketing.

It would be tasked with ensuring yaqona grown in and exported from Fiji meets regional and global quality standards.

The proposed Council would also formulate and implement certification and quality standards covering the cultivation, production, processing and marketing of yaqona.

Under the Bill, the Council could recommend fees and charges to the Minister for approval, including fees relating to registration and industry programmes.

It would work with relevant government departments, institutions and other stakeholders on matters affecting the yaqona industry, including assisting with the development and implementation of government policies.

The Council would also be responsible for developing research plans for the industry and improving capacity and efficiency across yaqona cultivation, production, processing, transportation and marketing.

It could facilitate funding assistance for research and marketing and gather and distribute information relevant to the industry.

Another key role would be advising or making recommendations to the Minister on matters relating to the yaqona sector.

The Council could also perform other functions assigned to it by the Minister.

The proposed registration and licensing regime forms part of the Bill’s wider attempt to establish a formal regulatory and management framework for Fiji’s yaqona industry.

item.title: 1,530 unresolved complaints before Legal Practitioners Unit
item.description: A total of 1,530 unresolved complaints dating as far back as 2009 are currently before the Legal Practitioners Unit. Acting Attorney-General and Minister for Justice Siromi Turaga revealed the figures in a written parliamentary response to Opposition Leader Inia Seruiratu.
item.content:encoded:
A total of 1,530 unresolved complaints dating as far back as 2009 are currently before the Legal Practitioners Unit.

Acting Attorney-General and Minister for Justice Siromi Turaga revealed the figures in a written parliamentary response to Opposition Leader Inia Seruiratu.

Mr Seruiratu had asked for the total number of unresolved complaints before the Legal Practitioners Unit, including a breakdown of the year in which each complaint was received.

“The total number of unresolved complaints currently before the Legal Practitioners Unit (LPU), together with a breakdown by the year in which each complaint was received,” Mr Turaga said in providing the figures.

The records show two complaints from 2009 remain unresolved, while 14 date back to 2010 and 16 to 2011.

The backlog increased significantly in subsequent years, with 44 unresolved complaints from 2012, 62 from 2013, 78 from 2014 and 89 from 2015.

There are also 96 unresolved complaints dating from 2016, 100 from 2017, 114 each from 2018 and 2020, and 116 from 2019.

More recent figures include 106 unresolved complaints from 2021, 122 from 2022, 120 from 2023 and 108 from 2024.

The largest number relates to 2025, with 132 unresolved complaints, while 97 complaints received in 2026 remain unresolved.

Mr Turaga also provided Parliament with an update on disciplinary proceedings before the Independent Legal Services Commission covering the period from October 31, 2025 to June 30, 2026.

“The figures capture all active and pending disciplinary proceedings between 31 October 2025 and 30 June 2026,” he said.

As of June 30, there were nine pending disciplinary cases.

Twelve new cases were registered or filed between November 1, 2025 and June 30, 2026, while three cases were disposed of or completed during the same period.

Of the nine pending matters, five involve professional misconduct applications and four involve unsatisfactory professional conduct applications.

One matter was awaiting judgment or a ruling after hearings had concluded and the decision had been reserved.

item.title: Officers can enter and inspect yaqona premises under new Bill
item.description: Enforcement officers would be given powers to enter and inspect premises used for yaqona operations under the Yaqona (Kava) Bill 2026. The proposed legislation would allow the Fiji Yaqona Council to appoint suitably qualified officers from the Ministry as enforcement officers to ensure compliance with the new law.
item.content:encoded:
Enforcement officers would be given powers to enter and inspect premises used for yaqona operations under the Yaqona (Kava) Bill 2026.

The proposed legislation would allow the Fiji Yaqona Council to appoint suitably qualified officers from the Ministry as enforcement officers to ensure compliance with the new law.

Under the Bill, enforcement officers could enter premises at any reasonable time when yaqona operations were being carried out.

This would cover premises used for the cultivation, processing, storage, importation or exportation of yaqona or yaqona products.

The definition of operations covered by the enforcement provisions includes cultivation, harvesting, storing, processing, pounding, packaging and activities associated with the manufacture of yaqona products.

Officers would also be empowered to inspect records, documents and information relating to activities regulated under the legislation.

They could require individuals to produce relevant records, documents or information and would be permitted to take copies of documents inspected during an enforcement operation.

The Bill would also give officers the power to take samples of yaqona or yaqona products.

Where problems are identified, an enforcement officer could require a person to take corrective measures relating to the cultivation, harvesting or storage of yaqona or yaqona products.

The proposed law states that a person “must comply with a lawful requirement” made by an enforcement officer.

Enforcement officers would be issued identification cards in a form approved by the Council and would be required to produce their identification when requested while exercising their powers.

The enforcement provisions form part of a wider regulatory framework proposed under the Bill, which would establish the Fiji Yaqona Council and introduce registration, licensing and standards for operators across Fiji’s yaqona industry.

item.title: FICAC received 407 complaints, secured 18 convictions in past year
item.description: The Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption received 407 complaints and recorded 18 successful convictions during the 12 months ending June 2026. Acting Attorney-General and Minister for Justice Siromi Turaga revealed the figures in a written parliamentary response to MP Jone Usamate.
item.content:encoded:
The Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption received 407 complaints and recorded 18 successful convictions during the 12 months ending June 2026.

Acting Attorney-General and Minister for Justice Siromi Turaga revealed the figures in a written parliamentary response to MP Jone Usamate.

Mr Turaga said FICAC dealt with 508 investigation files across its Suva, Lautoka and Labasa offices between July 1, 2025 and June 30, 2026.

“The Commission received a total of 407 complaints,” Mr Turaga said.

As of June 30, 182 investigation files remained active, with the majority being handled by the Suva office.

Of these, 125 were in Suva, 29 in Lautoka and 28 in Labasa.

Mr Turaga said another 141 matters were at the prosecution stage.

“In addition, 141 matters were at the prosecution stage. A further 19 matters were before the courts on appeal, bringing the total number of live court matters to 160,” he said.

The 19 appeal matters were recorded separately and were not included in the 141 cases at the prosecution stage.

On court outcomes, Mr Turaga said FICAC secured 18 successful convictions during the reporting period.

“The Commission recorded 18 successful convictions during the reporting period,” he said.

Mr Usamate had asked the Acting Attorney-General to provide Parliament with FICAC’s caseload statistics, including complaints received, investigations, prosecutions and successful convictions for the July 2025 to June 2026 period.

Mr Turaga said the figures reflected FICAC’s caseload and court outcomes for the relevant reporting period.

item.title: FICAC spent $19,022 on Pryde investigation and prosecution
item.description: The Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption spent approximately $19,022 on the investigation and prosecution of former Director of Public Prosecutions Christopher Pryde. The figure was revealed in a parliamentary response by Acting Attorney-General and Minister for Justice Siromi Turaga to a written question from Opposition Leader Inia Seruiratu.
item.content:encoded:
The Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption spent approximately $19,022 on the investigation and prosecution of former Director of Public Prosecutions Christopher Pryde.

The figure was revealed in a parliamentary response by Acting Attorney-General and Minister for Justice Siromi Turaga to a written question from Opposition Leader Inia Seruiratu.

Mr Seruiratu had asked the minister to inform Parliament of the total amount spent by FICAC investigating and prosecuting Mr Pryde.

According to the response, approximately $11,000 represented FICAC’s internal investigation and legal costs attributable to staff time.

A further $8,022 was incurred in New Zealand in relation to the service of court documents and associated processes.

“For context, the charges concerned an alleged total of $193,326.64, comprising alleged gratuity payments, alleged reimbursement monies received contrary to applicable procurement requirements, and alleged airline reimbursement monies,” Mr Turaga said.

It said FICAC’s estimated expenditure of $19,022 should be considered in the context of the nature and financial value of the matters that were the subject of the proceedings.

The disclosure comes after FICAC discontinued its legal proceedings against Mr Pryde in the Suva Magistrates Court last month. FICAC said at the time that it had been unable to effect service on Mr Pryde in New Zealand despite attempts to do so.

FICAC entered a nolle prosequi on July 22, bringing the existing proceedings to an end. The commission said the allegations against Mr Pryde had not been determined by the court and that the decision did not prevent subsequent proceedings based on the same facts.

The proceedings related to allegations concerning payments and reimbursements totalling $193,326.64 received during Mr Pryde’s tenure as DPP.
